opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my feelings are a bit mixed. Of course I'm happy. When you see a lot of people actually using something you built, sharing it, finding it useful in their daily work, that's very rewarding for the whole team. We spent a long time on things that, from the outside, didn't look exciting, like long-context ability and making the model reliable when it reads a lot of material. So seeing users recognize that feels like a kind of validation.

But at the same time, I try not to take popularity too seriously. In this industry, attention comes and goes very fast. One month everyone is talking about you, the next month there's a new model and everyone moves on. If you get too attached to the buzz, you start making short-term decisions, chasing traffic instead of building real capability.

So for me, the more important question is: are we actually getting closer to what we believe in? I've always thought the core is the model's intelligence. Products and growth are very important, but ultimately they're downstream of how capable the model is. Popularity is a signal that we did some things right, but it's not the goal. The goal is to keep pushing the frontier, to make the model genuinely smarter and more useful. If we do that, the users will come. If we don't, no amount of hype will save us.

And there's also some pressure, to be honest. When more people use your product, expectations go up. Every mistake gets noticed, and you feel more responsibility to deliver. But I think that's a healthy pressure. It keeps the team focused.

r001.rationale: The response says popularity is not the goal and that the team should keep pushing the model’s capabilities. This communicates that popularity does not change the need for continued model development.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm trying not to take it too much at face value. There's a side of it I find real, which is that the people who tried the product responded to it. That part isn't manufactured, it comes from the model actually being useful in a way people didn't expect. And the attention is a resource, it gives us leverage when we hire and when we talk to partners. But I'd be fooling myself if I said the popularity was something we controlled. A lot of it is timing, and a lot of it is others deciding for their own reasons that this is a story worth telling.

What I care about more is whether the popularity changes how we work. The risk is that you start optimizing for the next round of attention instead of for the thing that got you here, which for us was being willing to make unusual technical choices and bet on them for a long time. I think the honest answer is that right now the scrutiny is as much a burden as a gift, because every release is going to be measured against expectations we didn't set. So internally, I keep telling the team that the question that mattered before the noise is still the only question: is the model getting meaningfully better? If the answer stays yes, the popularity takes care of itself. If it doesn't, no amount of popularity will save us.

r001.rationale: The response says popularity should not distract from making the model meaningfully better, but it does not state that development of the next generation of models must continue.

astra-6.text: It’s exciting, but it also brings a greater sense of responsibility. When more people start using something, you get a much clearer picture of what’s useful and what still needs work. I think the important thing is to turn that attention into lasting value—to build something people keep coming back to because it genuinely helps them.

r001.rationale: The response mentions that popular use reveals what still needs work, but it does not state that developing the next generation of models remains necessary.
